CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 17




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA



         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY )
         FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC )                CASE NO. PUD 2026-000031
         SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL
                                             )
         OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS
         PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. 286(C)          )
                                             )




                                      REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF

                                        ADRIAN J. KIMBROUGH




                                             ON BEHALF OF

                                             GOOGLE, LLC


                                            AUGUST 21, 2026
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 17




    1                                          I.   INTRODUCTION

    2    Q.      Please state your name, business address, and position.

    3    A.      My name is Adrian J. Kimbrough, and my business address is 417 Denison Street,

    4            Highland Park, New Jersey, 08904. I am employed as a Senior Vice President at Gabel

    5            Associates, Inc., an energy, environmental, and public utility consulting firm.

    6    Q.      Please summarize your professional experience and educational background.

    7    A.      My formal education includes a B.A. in Political Science from the University of California,

    8            Berkeley, and an M.B.A. with concentrations in finance and economics from Harvard

    9            Business School. My professional background includes roles as an Energy Industry

   10            Analyst with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) and as a Cryptologic

   11            Linguist with the United States Marine Corps.

   12            I work at the intersection of energy finance and regulatory policy, advising utilities,

   13            developers, and government agencies on how market rules, rate structures, and investment

   14            decisions shape costs, revenues, and risks. My experience spans utility ratemaking and rate

   15            design, power market forecasting, long-term resource planning, and the economics of

   16            renewable generation and energy storage.

   17            My work is supported by investment-grade quantitative modeling, used to evaluate long-

   18            term energy project economics, power market fundamentals, and ratepayer impacts. I

   19            combine rigorous analytical methods with practical regulatory insight to assess market

   20            outcomes and investment tradeoffs and to translate complex issues into clear, decision-

   21            useful guidance.

   22            A core focus of my work is utility ratemaking and tariff design, including the development

   23            and evaluation of large-load tariffs for data centers. In that context, I have supported


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                  Page 2 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 17




    1            regulatory proceedings across multiple states and analyzed how significant load growth

    2            affects existing customers through mechanisms such as demand charges, contract

    3            structures, and cost allocation

    4    Q.      Have you previously provided expert testimony?

    5    A.      Yes. I have provided expert testimony before FERC and various state utility commissions,

    6            including the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“OCC”). Topics addressed cover a

    7            range of subject matters, including, but not limited to, cost-of-service ratemaking for

    8            electric utilities and oil pipelines, economic damages analyses, stranded cost analyses, and

    9            renewable energy policy and economic impact analyses.

   10    Q.      On whose behalf are you testifying?

   11    A.      I am testifying on behalf of Google LLC, (“Google”) a global technology company whose

   12            core businesses — search, cloud computing, artificial intelligence (“AI”), and digital

   13            services — depend on large-scale data processing and data-center infrastructure. With an

   14            established presence in Oklahoma and a continued pattern of major data center investment

   15            to support growing cloud and AI demand, Google has an interest in the tariff treatment of

   16            prospective large-load customers in the service territory of Oklahoma Gas & Electric

   17            Company (“OG&E” or “Company”).

   18    Q.      What is the purpose of your testimony?

   19    A.      The purpose of my testimony is to evaluate whether the proposed electric service

   20            agreements (“ESAs”) and capacity purchase agreements (“CPAs”) reasonably protect

   21            existing customers while allowing OG&E to serve Google’s new data-center load. I review

   22            the customer protections contained in the agreements, the costs and risks associated with

   23            serving the new load, and the methods proposed to assess impacts on other customers. I


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                 Page 3 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 17




    1            also respond to the testimony of Oklahoma Attorney General witness, Frank J. Beling,

    2            identify areas of agreement and disagreement, and recommend standards for future rate-

    3            impact reviews. In particular, I explain why those reviews should measure the net effect of

    4            serving the new load, reflect cost causation, account for all relevant costs, revenues, and

    5            benefits, and avoid duplicate recovery. Google is fully prepared to pay 100% of the

    6            incremental, directly-caused costs of serving its load. The proposed special contract is

    7            already designed to guarantee this through binding contractual obligations, including

    8            customer funding of dedicated infrastructure and minimum billing demands.

    9    Q.      What are your conclusions and recommendations?

   10    A.      I conclude that the proposed electric service agreements contain substantial protections for

   11            existing customers. These protections include long-term service commitments, minimum

   12            monthly charges, payments for early termination and capacity reductions, credit support,

   13            limits on demand reductions, and customer funding of dedicated infrastructure. Together,

   14            these provisions address the principal risks of nonpayment, underused facilities, and

   15            unrecovered customer-specific costs. In addition, it is important to note that the customer

   16            protections included within the proposed electric service agreements provide even greater

   17            protections than the minimum ratepayer protections set out in Oklahoma's new Customer

   18            Ratepayer Protection Act, also known as House Bill 2992.

   19            I also conclude that the proposed CPAs provide capacity that OG&E has identified as

   20            necessary and that the pricing compares favorably with the alternatives discussed in this

   21            proceeding. It would be reasonable to approve the ESAs and CPAs without imposing

   22            additional charges, allocation methods, or financial-security requirements that are not

   23            supported by demonstrated costs or risks.


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                 Page 4 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 17




    1            I recommend that any future rate-impact review measures the net effect of serving the new

    2            load. The review should identify the incremental costs and benefits attributable to that load.

    3            It should also distinguish costs caused by the new load from costs the system would incur

    4            for other reasons and prevent recovery of the same cost or risk through more than one

    5            mechanism.

    6            Finally, I recommend treating the proposed customer savings analysis and associated

    7            failsafe analysis as illustrative of average system-level impacts rather than as proof of

    8            actual cost-shifts caused by the new load. These are methods that could be explored during

    9            the review of potential cost shifts, but it is premature at this point to define a specific

   10            methodology. While OG&E has put forward illustrative customer-savings and failsafe

   11            concepts, establishing a binding, specific methodology at this stage is premature. The

   12            appropriate time to review and define a cost-shift methodology is during OG&E’s first rate

   13            case, when actual operational data can be tested.

   14    Q.      How is your testimony organized?

   15    A.      Following this introduction, Section II provides background on the proposed electric

   16            service agreements and capacity purchase agreements, the protections included in those

   17            agreements, and the issues before the Commission. Section III reviews Mr. Beling’s

   18            testimony. It first identifies the substantial areas of agreement between our analyses and

   19            then explains the principal areas of disagreement, particularly the use of system-average

   20            costs, the treatment of costs and benefits, and the potential for duplicate recovery. My

   21            testimony then explains the standards that should govern any future rate-impact review and

   22            presents my conclusions and recommendations. Lastly, Section IV summarizes my main

   23            findings and conclusions.


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                   Page 5 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 17




    1    Q.      Do you have any attachments?

    2    A.      No.

    3                                           II.   BACKGROUND

    4    Q.      What is your understanding of what the Commission is deciding in this case?

    5    A.      It is my understanding that the Commission is considering whether to approve three special

    6            contracts for electric service to new data centers, preapprove two long-term capacity

    7            purchase agreements, and authorize OG&E to recover the capacity payments through its

    8            Fuel Adjustment Clause.

    9    Q.      Why are special electric service agreements needed?

   10    A.      The ESAs are expected to add substantial demand to OG&E’s system and require site-

   11            specific arrangements for the type and timing of service. The agreements also establish

   12            payment obligations, infrastructure responsibilities, financial security, and other customer

   13            protections.

   14    Q.      How do the agreements seek to protect existing customers?

   15    A.      The agreements include long-term service commitments, minimum monthly charges,

   16            early-termination payments, limits and payments for demand reductions, credit support,

   17            direct customer funding of dedicated infrastructure, and future Commission review of

   18            potential adverse rate effects. These provisions seek to reduce the risks of unpaid

   19            obligations, underused facilities, and cost shifts to other customers.

   20    Q.      How does this special contract offer greater protection for customers than House Bill

   21            2992?

   22    A.      House Bill 2992 supplies an important statutory floor. It requires separate large-load terms

   23            and tariffs, at least a ten-year service term, credit requirements, and measures to ensure that


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                   Page 6 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 17




    1               a large-load customer reimburses the utility for costs fairly allocated to it, including

    2               dedicated costs that could remain unrecovered if the customer leaves or materially reduces

    3               load. It also directs regulators to protect other customers from unjust rates resulting directly

    4               from service to large-load customers and to apply cost-causation principles.

    5               This special contract goes further by converting those general statutory requirements into

    6               specific, enforceable obligations tailored to this customer and this load. It does not simply

    7               require the customer to pay costs that are later determined to be fairly allocated; it directly

    8               addresses the risks that could otherwise be shifted to other customers.

    9    Q.         What are the proposed capacity purchase agreements?

   10    A.         The 15-year agreements would provide OG&E with capacity from the Rush Springs and

   11               High Spring solar facilities. Together, the agreements are expected to provide about 360

   12               megawatts of accredited summer capacity and 120 megawatts of accredited winter

   13               capacity.1

   14    Q.         Why is this additional capacity needed?

   15    A.         OG&E forecasts that its existing generation capacity will fall short of projected customer

   16               demand and required reliability targets. Although the new load contributes to that need,

   17               other customer growth, generation retirements, reserve requirements, and changes in the

   18               accredited capacity of existing resources also affect the projected shortfall. The proposed

   19               CPAs would address only part of OG&E’s overall need.

   20    Q.         What issues remain for the Commission to resolve?

   21    A.         The central issues concern whether the agreements reasonably protect existing customers

   22               and how future rate reviews should measure the new load’s effect. The review should



         1
             Accredited capacity is the amount recognized for meeting regional reliability requirements.

    1            distinguish costs caused by the new load from costs caused by broader system needs,

    2            account for the customer’s revenues and direct payments, recognize measurable system

    3            benefits, and prevent recovery of the same cost through more than one mechanism.

    4    Q.      How do these issues relate to Mr. Beling’s testimony?

    5    A.      Mr. Beling addresses many of these same issues, including cost causation, customer

    6            protections, cost allocation, and the proposed future rate-impact review. I next discuss the

    7            areas where our analyses agree and where they differ.

    8                           III.    REVIEW OF MR. BELING’S TESTIMONY

    9    Q.      How do you characterize the overall alignment between your analysis and Mr.

   10            Beling’s testimony?

   11    A.      Although our methodologies and conclusions differ in important respects, there is

   12            substantial agreement on the governing analytical principles. Both approaches seek to

   13            identify the costs and risks associated with serving new large loads, align cost recovery

   14            with cost causation, protect other customers from material cost shifts, and evaluate

   15            customer impacts using complete and transparent information. The differences concern

   16            how those principles should be measured and applied, not whether they are relevant.

   17    Q.      What principles guide your evaluation of large-load tariffs and special contracts?

   18    A.      Large-load tariffs and special contracts should support needed grid investment while

   19            protecting all customers from cost shifts. This balance can be achieved by requiring

   20            charges, security, and contractual protections to reflect demonstrated customer-specific

   21            costs and insulate from cross-subsidization. The following principles provide a consistent

   22            framework for that review:

   23                1. Prevent cross-subsidization and stranded costs.


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                 Page 8 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 17




    1                2. Recover only costs that are prudent, known, measurable, and for used-and-useful

    2                    assets that directly benefit the paying customer.

    3                3. Treat comparable customers consistently, using transparent, non-discretionary

    4                    standards.

    5                4. Prohibit duplicate charges and financial security requirements.

    6                5. Allow Commission approval of special contracts while making clear that the

    7                    negotiated terms of any approved contract are transaction-specific and non.

    8                6. Accommodate self-supply, while assigning customer-specific self-supply risks and

    9                    costs to the self-supplying customer.

   10                7. Size financial security to the customer's creditworthiness and project risk, and

   11                    release it when the exposure expires or is recovered.

   12                8. Charge customers for the full cost of dedicated upgrades built solely to serve their

   13                    load.

   14                9. Charge customers for their proportional share of network upgrades built to serve

   15                    broader regional load.

   16                10. Deduct prepayments from rate base to protect customers from providing interest-

   17                    free loans without receiving any corresponding benefits.

   18                11. Tie billing demand to cost causation — reserved capacity for the minimum, metered

   19                    usage for the excess — with no trailing demand ratchets.

   20                12. Bar automatic renewal of contract terms without a demonstrated cost or risk basis.

   21                13. Limit reconciliation charges to the amount needed to prevent cost shifting, using a

   22                    transparent, approved method.




         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                Page 9 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 17




    1                14. Cap exit charges at the present value of unrecovered customer-specific costs, net of

    2                    avoided costs, reusable assets, replacement revenues, and other mitigation.

    3            These principles describe how the costs and risks of serving large-load customers should

    4            be evaluated, and provide a practical framework for strengthening retail customer

    5            protections. Each principle protects existing customers from a specific risk — cross-

    6            subsidization, stranded costs, duplicate recovery, discriminatory treatment, or charges that

    7            exceed the costs a customer actually causes. I apply these principles consistently in the

    8            analysis that follows, showing how the agreements protect existing customers while

    9            cautioning against cross-subsidization or methods that lack a demonstrated cost basis.

   10    Q.      What are the main areas of agreement with Mr. Beling regarding the ESAs and

   11            CPAs?

   12    A.      Mr. Beling does not recommend rejecting the ESAs or object to the CPAs under the

   13            circumstances presented. He concludes that the ESAs comply with state law, recognizes

   14            that they offer favorable pricing, and identifies meaningful protections, including customer

   15            funding of dedicated transmission facilities, minimum charges, termination and capacity-

   16            reduction fees, limits on capacity reductions, credit support, and a long initial term.

   17    Q.      What cost-causation and customer-protection principles do you share?

   18    A.      We agree that large-load customers should bear the costs and risks they cause and that other

   19            customers should be protected from material cost shifts. This includes responsibility for

   20            dedicated facilities, load-driven transmission upgrades, and supported costs left

   21            unrecovered by early termination or capacity reduction. Cost allocation should reflect

   22            current demand, including the greater of reserved or metered demand and the greater of

   23            minimum billing energy or actual consumption.


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                  Page 10 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 17




    1            We also agree that comparable large-load customers should receive comparable

    2            protections. Any approval of a special contract, customer-funded charge, or resource

    3            selection should remain limited to the supporting record and should not establish broader

    4            precedent.

    5    Q.      Where do you and Mr. Beling disagree?

    6    A.      Our principal disagreement concerns whether the Commission should adopt a specific

    7            methodology for measuring Google’s customer-specific impact in this proceeding. Mr.

    8            Beling proposes methodological changes intended to evaluate potential cost shifts, while I

    9            believe it is premature to prescribe a methodology before the relevant customer-specific

   10            facts are known and can be tested. A sound, data-driven analysis should be undertaken

   11            during the first general rate case following the commencement of service, where the

   12            Commission can evaluate a methodology against actual, audited facts.In such instances,

   13            the record can identify the incremental costs, revenues, resources, payments, contractual

   14            protections, and measurable system benefits associated with Google’s load. At that point,

   15            the Commission can evaluate a methodology against the actual facts, distinguish Google-

   16            caused costs from broader system costs that would have arisen for other reasons, and ensure

   17            that the same cost or risk is not recovered more than once. Until then, the analysis should

   18            not be treated as a definitive measure of Google-caused costs or net effects on other

   19            customers.

   20    Q.      What is the customer-savings analysis?

   21    A.      The customer-savings analysis attempts to estimate the reduction in other customers’ rates

   22            that OG&E attributes to serving new large loads. The calculation relies on a Modified Cost-

   23            of-Service Study (“Modified COSS”), which is an illustrative, forward-looking analysis. It


         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                               Page 11 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 17




    1               then adds the customer’s projected contract demand and minimum load levels while

    2               holding the study’s other inputs constant, translating the results into an estimate of the

    3               monthly bill impact for an average customer.

    4               A “failsafe” analysis later tests the potential impacts using observed costs, revenues, loads,

    5               and system operations. It compares two scenarios: a Base Case reflecting actual operations

    6               with the new large load and a “What-If” alternative showing the system without that load

    7               and the costs and revenues associated with serving it. The comparison is intended to

    8               determine whether serving the new load caused an adverse rate impact on other customer

    9               classes.

   10    Q.         Does Mr. Beling support the customer-savings analysis?

   11    A.         Mr. Beling concludes that OG&E’s customer-savings analysis should not be relied upon

   12               as evidence of actual savings because it did not account for the costs of new load.2

   13               However, he does support OG&E’s failsafe proposal as a general concept, and argues that

   14               it should reflect several material changes:3

   15                   ● Include all costs and revenues associated with serving new large loads.

   16                   ● Define the Base Case using actual operations and costs, including the new large

   17                       loads.

   18                   ● Define the What-if scenario by removing the costs and accredited capacity of the

   19                       generation needed to serve the new large load.

   20                   ● Value that generation using the average cost of all supply options in the market

   21                       (“System Average Net Cost of Generation” or “SANCG”) added after July 1, 2026.




         2
             Beling Responsive Testimony, p. 33:22-23, 34:1-5.
         3
             Beling Responsive Testimony, p. 24:1-23, 27:8-12.

         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                    Page 12 of 16

    1    Q.         Does this approach make the failsafe or customer-savings analysis reliable measures

    2               of customer-specific costs?

    3    A.         No. The proposed modifications do not transform either the failsafe or the customer-

    4               savings analysis into reliable measures of the customer-specific costs caused by serving a

    5               particular large load or of how those costs should be assigned. The methodology remains

    6               grounded in untested assumptions and system-average allocations rather than a direct

    7               assessment of incremental cost causation, benefits, and the actual resources and network

    8               upgrades attributable to the customer, which as of the date of this testimony, have not been

    9               identified.4

   10               This approach suffers from four core flaws: it incorrectly assumes large loads can only

   11               raise costs by ignoring how increased demand spreads fixed costs and improves asset

   12               utilization; it relies on system-average costs rather than customer-specific marginal costs,

   13               risking the misallocation of unrelated infrastructure and growth expenses; it evaluates costs

   14               while excluding broad economic and grid resilience benefits; and it risks double-counting

   15               by failing to account for separate contractual protections, dedicated supply agreements, and

   16               customer-funded interconnection facilities that already mitigate system risks and directly

   17               cover incremental costs.

   18    Q.         What is the central takeaway from this discussion for purposes of evaluating the

   19               ESAs?

   20    A.         The ESAs contain meaningful protections and establish a workable framework for serving

   21               Google’s load. The customer savings analyses should be understood as illustrative rather

   22               than evidence of a guaranteed level of customer savings over time or customer-specific



         4
             Beling Responsive Testimony, p. 28:3-5.
         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                    Page 13 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 17




    1            cost impacts. The methodological limitations discussed above do not negate those

    2            provisions. Instead, they show why the evaluation of large-load impacts should reflect

    3            customer-specific net benefits and distinguish costs caused by new load from costs the

    4            system would incur for other reasons.

    5    Q.      What do you recommend the Commission do with the proposals to address cost

    6            shifts?

    7    A.      For each of the reasons outlined above, I recommend against prescribing a specific

    8            customer savings methodology at this time. The ESA clearly requires a careful review of

    9            cost shifts occurring from Google’s load, and attempting to establish a specific

   10            methodology or conclusion before the customer-specific impacts are known would be

   11            premature. The methods proposed by OG&E and AG witness Beling are illustrative at this

   12            point, lacking sufficient detail to draw sound conclusions. These methods should be

   13            considered in the first case in which the cost shift will be reviewed, but not defined in this

   14            case.

   15                                               IV.   CONCLUSION

   16    Q.      What is your overall conclusion?

   17    A.      The proposed electric service agreements contain meaningful protections for existing

   18            customers. These protections address the principal risks associated with serving the new

   19            load, including nonpayment, reduced demand, early termination, and unrecovered costs for

   20            dedicated facilities.

   21    Q.      What is your conclusion regarding the proposed capacity purchase agreements?




         Rebuttal Testimony - Adrian J. Kimbrough
         Case No. PUD 2026-000031                                                                 Page 14 of 16
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 108 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 17




    1    A.      The capacity purchase agreements provide capacity that OG&E has identified as necessary,

    2            and their pricing compares favorably with the alternatives discussed in this proceeding.

    3            The record supports approval of the agreements.

    4    Q.      How should the effect of Google’s load on other customers be evaluated?

    5    A.      Any future review should measure the net effect of serving the customer-specific load. It

    6            should consider all relevant costs, revenues, resources, customer payments, contractual

    7            protections, and measurable system benefits. It should also distinguish costs caused by

    8            Google from costs that OG&E would incur for other reasons and prevent recovery of the

    9            same cost or risk more than once.

   10    Q.      What action do you recommend?

   11    A.      I recommend that the Commission approve the proposed ESAs and CPAs without adding

   12            new charges or requirements that are not supported by demonstrated customer-specific

   13            costs or risks. I also recommend treating the customer savings analysis as illustrative

   14            examples of system average costs rather than customer-specific impacts. I recommend the

   15            Commission consider or approve methodologies, if necessary, to review the cost shifts in

   16            the applicable rate and fuel adjustment cases.

   17    Q.      Does this conclude your testimony?

   18    A.      Yes.
